lines.note: The left running header reads M ANTES DO I.; the decorated initial is M rather than OCR N. No printed page number is present in this header.

runs.text: Ley ſecreta que ſe enſina em particular

lines.note: This mippoo denotes a secret doctrine taught privately, distinct from the honeybee homograph at the end of f321. It begins a normal flush-left entry, anticipated by that page's catchword.
The private doctrine is taught through points for meditation. This completes the preceding definition rather than introducing a separate practice-name.
Mippu is explained by maotoko, an adulterous male partner. The scan has initial M in Mauotoco, not OCR N; the woman's relation to him is described below.
Completes the description of a man with whom a woman has an illicit partnership. Upright S. labels written usage; molher is retained as printed.
Miken is the space between the eyebrows, explained by mayu no aida. En- begins entre below; the headword has been returned to the entry margin.
Completes entre as duas sobrancelhas, between the two eyebrows. The short Portuguese continuation finishes the anatomical definition.

runs.text: Vinho, falando com reſpeito, ou reuerẽ-

lines.note: Miki is a respectful term for wine or sake. Reſpeito has a t, not OCR l; the abbreviated reuerẽ- continues the word for reverence on the next row.

runs.text: cia dalgum grande ſenhor, ou Fotoque.

lines.note: The respectful reference is to a great lord or a Buddha. Fotoque occurs within the Portuguese explanation; the gloss qualifies the register of miki rather than specifying a different beverage.
Mikiki, mikiku and the printed past ending ijta mean seeing and hearing. Qe- begins kerai, the attendants whose behaviour is described in the following example.

runs.text: raino monodomo cague yori miqiqu. Mõ.

lines.note: Kerai no monodomo kage yori mikiku describes household attendants seeing and hearing from concealment. Enlargement shows the final citation as Mõ., with a short wavy nasal mark rather than the draft's caron; the small mark is weak, and the cited source is not identified here.

runs.text: A gente de caſa via, & ouuia às eſcondidas.

lines.note: The household people watched and listened secretly. The visible forms ouuia and eſcondidas correct OCR outia and ejcondidas and match the Japanese paired verb.

runs.text: Ver bem, ou de todo algũa

lines.note: Mikiri, mikiru and mikitta concern seeing something thoroughly or completely. The object of the Portuguese definition follows below.
Ikusa no yoosu wo mikiru is fully discerning the situation of a battle. The scan supports yǒſuuo, with the object particle uo after yǒſu, not the OCR's extra n in yǒſunuo.

runs.text: totalmente o que ha de paſſar na batalha.

lines.note: Completes ver: perceiving fully what is to happen in the battle. Totalmente replaces OCR tatalmente, and the whole Portuguese word batalha is italic, including its final a.
Mikiwame means seeing perfectly or bringing observation to completion. Its supplied principal parts are preserved rather than replaced with modern inflectional notation.
Completes the alternative explanation as finishing seeing. This is the end of the mikiwame entry, before the separate burial term below.

runs.text: Sepultura de peßoa nobre, ou ſãcta.

lines.note: Mikan is a burial place or tomb of a noble or holy person. Sepultura is one word in the scan, not the OCR's Se pultura; the printed nasal abbreviation in ſãcta is preserved.
Mirai is the future, explained literally as not yet having come. The repeated Mirai- begins an example that continues below with its object particle.
Mirai wo kangayuru is considering or conjecturing about the future. Lançar begins the idiom lançar contas on the following row.

runs.text: contas ſobre o que à de vir.

lines.note: Completes the explanation as reckoning about what is to come. The printed à de vir is retained without inserting a modern h.
Miraise is the future world, explained by the world or age that has not yet come. The scan reads Mũdo futuro, with a nasal abbreviation, rather than OCR Mido futuno.
This phrase describes a future age or world whose duration is qualified below. The printed yǒgo is retained without adding an accent to its final vowel.
The future age is not to end. This establishes an everlasting-future sense for the preceding expression.
Mirai yǒyǒ is equated with the preceding everlasting-future expression. Both printed carons are retained; Idem supplies the definition by reference.
Miren is explained as not yet being seasoned or trained, then glossed as cowardice. Mirẽ- is an upright Japanese nasal abbreviation beginning the example, not an italic Portuguese fragment.
Miren wo kamayuru is glossed as being cowardly. The entry then introduces its more exact explanation with the divided Portuguese ſẽ-tido, sense.

runs.text: tido deſta palaura he liuiandade de homem que

lines.note: Completes sentido and describes the instability or fickleness of a person. The following rows explain the behaviour rather than simply repeating the short cowardice gloss.

runs.text: ſe arremeßa, ou altera facilmente, mas no milhor

lines.note: The person rushes forward or becomes excited easily, but fails at the decisive moment. This is an indented continuation, not a new unindented entry.
The person fails, loses heart, or flees. Foge has a visible f cross-stroke and supplies the required fleeing sense, correcting OCR ſoge.
Mirengi has the same cowardice sense. Kamaite introduces an emphatic warning whose object is divided across mirengui- and uo below.
The warning is not to display cowardice. Qir. is the upright citation label; Guardai is one word despite damage to its r, and mos- begins mostreis below.
Completes mostreis couardia, show cowardice, within the preceding prohibition. The brief row closes the cited example.
Mirenna hito is a cowardly person. The initial M of the headword is clear in the scan, correcting OCR Nirenna; the following indented forms belong to this word family.
Mirenni supplies the adverbial form of the preceding cowardice term. No separate Portuguese definition is printed on this short indented row, and none is supplied in the transcription.
Mirensa supplies the abstract -sa form, the quality or degree of the preceding characteristic. It remains a separate indented physical row with no invented gloss.

runs.text: Hũs limos domar que ſe comem.

lines.note: Miru denotes edible seaweed, described as sea growths that people eat. The scan supports Hũs limos domar que ſe comem, replacing the severely garbled OCR; Hũs and joined domar remain diplomatic spellings.
Mirume directs the reader to the entry Mi, miru, the verb of seeing. Vide is the italic cross-reference instruction; the cited Japanese principal forms remain upright.
Mirumiruto is labelled an adverb and glossed as vividly or freshly. Its sense is illustrated by a person's youthful appearance in the next rows.
The example says that someone still looks strikingly fresh and young. The historical vacǒ and vomiyearu spellings are retained rather than converted to modern wakaku and mieru.

runs.text: Ainda parece muito freſco, & mancebo nas

lines.note: The person still looks very fresh and young. Nas introduces the complexion or colouring mentioned on the following row.
Completes nas cores, in complexion or colouring. This closes the youthful-appearance example rather than naming a new entry.
Misabi is said to be used commonly in the past tense. The grammatical comment continues across the divided pre-terito before explaining the loss of freshness in the thing seen.

runs.text: terito por ver algũa couſa friamente não lhe

lines.note: Completes preterito and describes looking at something coolly or without former enthusiasm. The negative judgment continues below with what the observer no longer finds in it.
The observer no longer finds the thing's earlier charm. Printed ja and joined deprimeiro are preserved, not modernized or resegmented.
Misadame is determining or establishing something by looking. The example following Vt concerns ascertaining where a person lives.

Hito no sumika wo misadamuru is identifying a person's dwelling. The damaged initial is read as F from the remaining strokes and the coherent hito phrase, rather than OCR citono; its impression is weak.

runs.text: cair bem no lugar onde hum està, ou mora.

lines.note: Completes the explanation as accurately recognizing the place where someone is or lives. The row is a continuation at the inset margin, not an independent entry.
The right running header repeats M ANTES DO I., with a capital I. It is page furniture, not a dictionary entry, and no page number is supplied where the scan has none.
Misago names the bird here glossed as guincho; the initial M and long s are visible. This is a new flush-left headword, not a continuation from the opposite column.

Misageru first means looking downward; the paragraph mark introduces another sense on the following row. The printed abbreviation Itẽ and the old preposition pera are retained, and the headword is flush left.

The second sense is looking contemptuously at someone, illustrated by Fitouo misaguru. Both the long s of desprezo and the example's misaguru are consistent with the visible types; the Japanese example remains roman.
This Portuguese translation completes the example: seeing someone while despising them. The joined object-pronoun spelling desprezandoo is printed and is not expanded or hyphenated.

runs.text: O não estar a couſa a-

lines.note: Misai is explained by imada sumazu, something not yet settled or clarified. The final a- belongs to the Portuguese word continued on the next row; the local estar spelling is retained rather than imposing a long-s form.
Clarada completes a-clarada, followed by aueriguada, making the sense 'not clarified or ascertained.' The physical division and historical u spelling are preserved.

This separate misai entry gives misaina as an alternative and describes minute or particular matters. The separator is the printed l, rather than an added equivalence word; meuda and the par- division remain literal.
After the end of particular, the example begins Misaina cotouo na voxera-. The negative construction continues with reso on the next row; its split is not repaired into a single physical line.

runs.text: Não digais miudezas que tirão pera

lines.note: Reso completes the preceding voxera- in the prohibition. The Portuguese warns against speaking petty details tending toward baseness, retaining miudezas, tirão and pera as printed.
The one-word continuation completes the preceding Portuguese sentence. Its indentation and final period distinguish it from an independent entry.

Misauo is paraphrased as mono no kawaranu koto, absence of change. The scan shows Monono with initial M, not the OCR Nonono, and only one period after the italic P label; the final O begins the Portuguese definition below.
This completes O não auer mudança, 'there being no change.' The historical auer spelling is preserved without adding a modern h.

runs.text: Certa confeição de grãos, arroz, & ſal

lines.note: Miso is defined as a preparation of grains or beans, rice and salt. The printed confeição and grãos are retained; the definition continues into the next row rather than ending at sal.

runs.text: com que ſe tempera o Xiru de Iapão.

lines.note: The preparation seasons Japanese Xiru, an embedded Japanese noun within the Portuguese explanation. Xiru appears in the surrounding italic type here and is listed for human typeface review; Iapão is left in its historical spelling.
Misoca is glossed as the last day of the month. The P label and Portuguese definition are italic in this row; the unaccented mes is not modernized.
Misocana is the adjectival form for something secret. The final P belongs to the printed entry, and the long s of secreta is retained with the italic Portuguese phrase.
Misocani is explicitly the adverb, 'secretly.' The Adu. and P. labels accompany italic Portuguese, while the headword remains roman; no accent is supplied to the Japanese ending.

runs.text: Ceſto por onde coão o Miſò.

lines.note: Misocoxi is a basket used for straining miso. The second Miſò is embedded in Portuguese and carries a visible grave, unlike the unaccented beginning of the headword; its italic appearance is preserved and flagged for font review.
Misodate is defined as supporting or raising someone under one's observation. The unusual paradigm tçuru is what is printed and is not regularized to an expected modern conjugation.
The Portuguese definition ends with raising someone in one's sight, then the Japanese example begins 'that child until now.' The object sequence couo and the joined imamade are kept as printed.
Misodateta completes the example of having raised the child until now. The Portuguese begins Tègora, with a grave over e, and uses the historical minino rather than an editorially modernized menino.
This completes the translation with giving the child affection or treats. The separate lhe and the abbreviation &c. are visible and retained without adding a pronoun hyphen.
Misoqi is glossed literally as thirty-three years. Whatever a later lexical analysis may expect, the scan clearly has tres and annos; the definition is not corrected to a different numeral.

The headword is Miſome, not the OCR Miſore: the small middle letter has the remaining minims of m. Mifajimuru and the Portuguese 'begin to see' support that scan reading; this entry must remain distinct from Miſore below.
The short indented row completes Começar de ver. Its period ends the Misome definition and is not part of the following headword.

Misonji means erring in what one sees. The example starts the personal name Bẽ- in roman type; the nasalized e belongs to the same name rather than a separate italic run, and the division is preserved.

runs.text: qei moxi mata miſonzuru fodo naraba,

lines.note: Qei completes the preceding Bẽ-; the conditional example continues with moxi mata misonzuru fodo naraba. The scan has q rather than g, and the entire sentence remains a Japanese example, not embedded Portuguese terminology.

runs.text: ſaigono caiuo tatta fitotçu fucǒzu. Tog.

lines.note: The example ends with blowing the final shell once; fucǒzu has a downward-pointing caron over o. Tog. is a printed roman citation label after the Japanese sentence and is separately listed for human font review.

runs.text: Bẽquei diſſe ſe por ventura não acertar de ver

lines.note: The Portuguese repeats the name as Bẽquei, with qu rather than the preceding Japanese qei spelling, and begins the conditional translation. This occurrence of the name is inside Portuguese prose and is italic in the scan; its differing spelling is retained.

runs.text: bem o que paßa, ſòmente darei ſinal da morte

lines.note: The translation continues with giving only the signal of death if one fails to see what is happening. Enlargement separates the grave over the o of ſòmente from the head of the preceding long s; the source's paßa and ſinal are preserved.
The translation concludes with sounding the shell. Buzio is printed without a written accent, and the final period closes the extended Misonji example.
This distinct Misore entry means forgetting or not recognizing what one has seen. The last mark is a line-end hyphen after conhe-, not the OCR period; its continuation belongs to the next row.

runs.text: cer o quetinha viſto, como quem paßa por alguẽ

lines.note: Cer completes conhe- before the object o, then the definition describes passing someone previously seen. A small word space before o is visible; the locally joined quetinha and the nasal abbreviation alguẽ are retained rather than normalized.

runs.text: ſem lhe falar por não o conhecer bem.

lines.note: The example describes passing without speaking because one does not recognize the person well. The printed lhe remains separate and the sentence ends on this continuation row.
Misori gives a different error of sight or judgment, thinking someone has good qualities. The paradigm ends otta, with doubled t, and the Portuguese cuidando continues syntactically below.

runs.text: dalguem q̃ he bom, ou tẽ algũas boas partes,

lines.note: This continues 'of someone that he is good or has some good qualities.' The scan's q̃ and tẽ are abbreviations, not damaged words to expand; algũas keeps its tilde over u.
The short final clause makes clear that the favorable judgment is mistaken. The ampersand and joined reflexive enganandoſe are preserved on their own indented physical row.

The bird entry begins Miſoſanzai with M, not OCR N, and recommends Mizoſanzai after Meliùs. The latter is a standalone lexical alternative, not a Japanese term inside Portuguese prose; the punctuation after Meliùs is a comma in the scan.
Nho completes Paßari- and the definition simply calls it a bird so named. The row is visibly inset, so its missing continuation indentation is restored without changing the physical division.
Misoya is a place selling miso. The second Miſò has a grave and is embedded in the italic Portuguese definition, unlike the ordinary headword; it is listed for human font review.

runs.text: Iguaria de Xiru, em que metẽ

lines.note: The headword is the uninterrupted compound Miſoyaqijiru; the OCR space between j and iru is not supported by a word break. Xiru occurs within the Portuguese description of the dish and is italic here; metẽ carries a nasal abbreviation.
The dish contains Tofus and finely cut radish. Tofus is an embedded Japanese food term printed in the surrounding italic, while the Portuguese rabão is left unmodernized.
Misôzzu recommends Zôſui as the better form, with visible circumflexes in both. The standalone equivalent is roman; the comma after Meliùs and the Portuguese co- division are preserved.

runs.text: mo dieta de eruas, arroz, Miſò, &c.

lines.note: Mo completes co-mo and describes a dish of herbs, rice and miso. The indented continuation has embedded italic Miſò, with its printed grave, and is not an independent headword.
Missô is paraphrased as secretly addressing a superior. The headword preserves its mixed long and short s and circumflex, while mǒxi has a caron; the Portuguese ſe- is visibly divided at the row end.

runs.text: gredo a peſſoa nobre, como a Rey, &c.

lines.note: Gredo completes ſe-gredo, specifying a noble recipient such as a king. This continuation is inset in the scan, and Rey retains its capital and historical spelling.

runs.text: Esteiras que ſe poem nas janelas, varã-

lines.note: Misu denotes mats or blinds placed at windows and verandas. The final varã- has a nasal abbreviation and continues on the next body row; the headword is flush left and is not part of the catchword.

The visible lowercase das completes varã-das, replacing OCR Nas. The far-right Miſuca- on the same baseline is separate page furniture, moved to a new catchword ID rather than included in this Portuguese body row.
The far-right catchword anticipates the Miſucaxi entry on the next page. It shares the last body baseline but is not part of the definition of Miſu; the printed hyphen remains.
